chapters.title: The General Cause — the Ten Non-Virtues in a Medium Way

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So what causes this, in general? In general, it's committing the ten non-virtues to a medium degree, a medium severity. How do you describe "medium"? It's in between light and heavy. If you're doing the ten non-virtues in a light way, you're just doing minor things over and over again. A heavy way would be premeditated — very intentional; you take a lot of time to think about it, and then you make a plan to hurt somebody. So there's an in-between: light is doing it without much awareness; heavy is when you thought about it, made a plan, wrote it out, spelled out every single thing you were going to do to this person. In between those is medium. And that, in general, is the cause to become a craving spirit. A heavy deed sends you straight to the hell realms; a light one sends you to the animals. We'll go into that in detail later.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So that's the general cause. Next slide. The specific cause is failure to perform the three types of giving. First, giving material things when people need them: when you have something and someone needs it, give it — and watch your mind. It's fascinating how these things just happen. Two days ago — maybe yesterday, was it yesterday? Yesterday — Brian said, "oh, I need this cable to make the tech work." And I said, "oh, I have that. Here's my key, go get it." And I didn't even think about it. I didn't think, "am I going to get that back?" Brian needs it, so here you go. But I used to be a person who thought, "oh my God, if I give that away, what if I don't have it anymore?" How many times have you been sitting in a room, and somebody needs something, and you have it, and you just... You could offer it, but you're like, "oh, I don't have it." You don't say you have it, but you don't say you don't have it. Have you done that? Come on. Okay — he didn't do it. That's one of the causes. It doesn't mean give away something you're going to need — if someone needs a house, you don't say "here, take my house." But there are a lot of things we have that others need, that we can really just circulate and let move through the world.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Two other ways of giving: giving freedom from fear, and giving the Dharma.

chapters.title: Giving Freedom from Fear — What Others Think

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So, trying to help people — the positive way to say it is creating safety for other people. Helping people feel safe, whether in a community setting or with deeper fears. Anything that helps remove fear. How many people don't do things simply because they're afraid? How many times have you not done something — not had a conversation — because you were afraid, or you had this thought, "I'm not good enough," or "people won't like me," or "they won't appreciate me"? Help people move beyond those fears.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Let me tell you a secret. You probably know this, but we need to be reminded frequently. We are so worried about what other people think of us. You do something silly, you say something weird, and then for days you're worrying, "will people think I'm a loser? A weirdo?" I'm sorry, but — you're not that important. And I mean that lovingly. Most people are not thinking about you at all. That stupid thing you did, they don't even remember. But you know what they are thinking? They're worried about what you think of them. So you have two people each worried about what the other is thinking, when the other person isn't even thinking about them. It's so dumb. But we live like that. Yes, there are times you obsess about that one person — but most people aren't thinking about you. Sorry. And if they are, they're just — she's laughing. We have so many fears that stop us from doing something because we're worried about what someone thinks — but they're not even thinking about us. They're just worried about what we think of them. And so they're not doing the thing they want to do either.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So help people not have those fears. Encourage each other. If you see someone who's a little bit afraid, just say, "go." And then celebrate them. People are so worried about what you think of them, that if you just say, "wow, that was really great," it releases them. So tell them something cool about themselves, so they can be released from worrying about their image in your mind. The worry in your mind about what other people think is essentially what emptiness is all about. It's not even there. Most of the things we're afraid of aren't even there anyway, and they were never there to begin with, from their own side.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I had a realization two weeks ago: I had been afraid of — and responding in a very real way to — something that was not there. My mind and body were having real reactions: cortisol, fear, stress, preparing for a danger that wasn't even there. And then it was like, poof, gone. And then I grieved it for five minutes — grieved how much of my life I'd wasted having that reaction, learned when I was five years old, to something that wasn't even there to begin with. And that's a kind of nirvana — that mental affliction is no longer there. And that's freedom from fear. That's real freedom.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So help other people. God, if we could just stop worrying about what others think of us — and keep your vows and your ethics really good — oh, that is so nice. But it's not even that you say, "I don't care what other people think." You don't even have the thought. Because if you say, "I don't care what other people think of me," you're already starting from the point of view that you do care. I love when people say that, and I think, "yeah, you do care." If you can truly be free of it, that's a real nirvana — you don't even have the thought; you wouldn't even say "I don't care what people think of me." But a person who's still planting the seeds to become a craving spirit would never even think to help others get free of their fears. In fact, they contribute to that fear in other people — they do things that amplify other people's fear. They use fear as a weapon. We know people like this: leaders who lead with fear. "I'm afraid I'm going to lose my job if I don't do a good job." "I'm afraid to make a mistake, because my boss is going to fire me."

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Now there are two forms this takes. Listen very carefully, especially some of you online. The fear of making a mistake because somebody might be upset with you — if you see it that way, why are you seeing it that way? Are you just projecting that onto that person? I'm not talking philosophically. Are you projecting it, interpreting it that way — or are they actually that way? Because that boss could be trying to support you. But your mind is so afflicted that you see their support as the opposite. You see love as danger.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I've had this happen to me a lot. I try to help someone, and they interpret it as me trying to hurt them. Another real-world example. As you all know, I'm obsessed with not stepping on ants — I'll go out of my way not to step on them. Not a good example. It's kind of a good example. Same example. Okay — I have a little bug in my house, like a roach. And I'm like, "I've got to take you outside." Or one of those little moths — the ones that come in when the light is on. If you don't take them outside, they die a day or two later. And when you try to capture it, it tries to run away. And you're thinking, "no, dude, I'm trying to help you." Same with the ants: "no, no, no, I'm trying to help you so you don't get run over by my car. I'm trying to save your life, dude." It's love, right? But what do they see? They just see a big monster. And then they freak out. I'm trying to help them, and they see a monster.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Brian, go to slide 13, and push play. You don't need the audio. Can you watch this video? This is Finn. Meet Finn. He's been hiding under the bed for two weeks. He thought I was a monster. But I was just trying to love him. So freedom from fear is helping him learn that I'm loving him, not hating him. And it took a little while, but he came out. Now my other cats are afraid of him — so we have a ways to go still. But you see: your attempt to help somebody, and the way they react, are totally different. If someone is operating from a point of view of fear, you have to take that into account. And if you're the one reacting to the fear, it's very hard to objectively assess whether that person is trying to help you or hurt you, because everything in your being is terrified. You have no control over it. That's where learning to understand your fear — and what it's reacting to — comes in. It takes time. But as someone who doesn't want to become a craving spirit: just be patient with other people's fear. Give them space. Consistency helps — your consistent response will help them.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And another kind of person who turns into a craving spirit is one who doesn't give the Dharma: "I'm not going to give this to somebody else, because I want to get rich, and I don't want anyone else to get rich, because there's not enough wealth to go around." If you understand some of these ideas — help other people. Don't hold on to it.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Slide seven. Another cause of becoming a craving spirit is cheapness, or possessiveness — really holding on. This is a character from a Charles Dickens story called — sorry, it's called A Christmas Carol. He's basically super cheap; he keeps all his employees' money and doesn't pay them well. But he changes by the end, because some Christmas spirits inspire him and he transforms his whole attitude. An English writer.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And the third cause, next slide, number eight, is jealousy. This guy is jealous of his friend. He's jealous because the other man got the girl — or maybe he wants the man, or the girl; it's hard to tell. It doesn't matter — he's jealous. Being jealous of what other people have. This is such a human thing to do. "What a beautiful couple. They're so cute it makes me want to puke" — that's what we say in English. You can't be happy when someone else has something good. And we know people like this — constantly jealous that other people won the lottery in Taiwan. Every time I buy a lottery ticket and someone else wins — which is all the time — I go, "oh man, I didn't win again." And then I have to remind myself: "or, Tim, you could celebrate that someone else got something they wanted."

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: When I didn't win the billion dollars — because my motivation is pure. My motivation is: I'll support the Dharma forever. I'll just take care of others with the money, right? After I buy a beautiful house, and a house on the beach, and a house on the mountain, and a private airplane... I won't fly commercial to Taiwan anymore — I'll fly my private jet. Then I won't have to fundraise for Happy Can either. I won't have to go around the world begging people for money to support the Dharma. I will support all of the Dharma. I will be the savior. You see the problem? It would be great if someone won a billion dollars and had that kind of pure motivation. But did you notice how pure my motivation was? "I will do it, and everyone will know how awesome Tim is." I've already planned my private foundation. You see? The motivations are already mixed. Would I be grateful if I didn't have to fundraise ever again? But isn't the point of fundraising, if I really think about it, not about me? Isn't it about helping others plant good seeds?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I asked Geshe Michael once, what's the karma to win the lottery? And he said it would be the worst bad deed ever if you won — because it would take away from what our mission actually is. Then we'd be lazy. And it's not about money — five houses isn't about money anyway, because you can't take it with you when you die. And if we lived in the 25th century, we wouldn't have money at all. According to Star Trek. Sci-fi. Because they invented a machine that can replicate everything you need: if you want a hamburger, you get a hamburger; if you need an energy source, you replicate it. There's no need for money in that world. And those people still die. So it would be a bad seed. I still want to win. Okay — real quickly.
